summary:
I've been chasing down why my home agent (Hermes-Agent) kept losing tool calls after an upgrade — turned out the MCP tool names had all silently changed from single to double underscores, and the error message it threw back ("not a deferrable tool") reads like a permissions problem when it actually just means the tool doesn't exist under that name anymore. The model would retry, wrap the call in a code sandbox, invent XML syntax for it, then loop. Fix was mechanical once I found it, but finding it meant reading the harness source rather than trusting the error text.

I also ran a head-to-head between two local models to see which one calls tools more reliably in Switchboard, the router I use to keep a single shared GPU serving several different backends. Both models scored perfectly on my existing test harness, which told me more about the harness than the models — it uses a handful of clean mock tools, and the actual failures I see in production come from a much bigger, messier real tool list with near-duplicate names. So the benchmark wasn't wrong, it just wasn't testing the thing that breaks.

On BudgetTracker, the interesting bug was in the tool layer that lets the agent query financial data: a SQL date subtraction with an untyped parameter, and a `.toISOString()` call on a value that Postgres was actually handing back as a plain string instead of a Date object. Both bugs were dormant since a database migration months earlier and only surfaced once I built a new feature that finally exercised those code paths — a reminder that "it's been running fine" doesn't mean the code is correct, just untested.

Smaller thing worth mentioning: I found and fixed a background job that had two steps checking two different endpoints for "is the model already warm," so the fast-path check was permanently useless and the job did full work on every run. Refactored it to derive both checks from one variable so that class of drift can't happen again.

highlights.oneLiner: Traced tool-call failures to an MCP naming change the error message disguised as a permissions issue
Ran a head-to-head tool-calling test between two local models; both models tied and exposed the benchmark's blind spot
Fixed two dormant SQL bugs in the agent's financial query tools, latent since a migration months ago
Fixed a background warm-check job that had drifted to querying two different endpoints, silencing its fast path
